title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 9-12
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up lines 9 to 12 of Shitou's Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, opening with Shitou's awakening and a dream of riding a tortoise with Huineng across the sea. Joden compares several translations and reads the Chinese characters, tracing "ten square feet" to the fangzhang, the size of Vimalakirti's room, where Manjushri and a crowd of guests find space while Shariputra worries about a chair. Participants read the hut as a practice, as the self, or as a park bench, and weigh the line "the middling or lowly can't help wondering" against the hierarchical societies the poem came from. Breakout rooms return with the idea that practice is portable and with the trouble of explaining practice to people who don't sit.

sentences.text: Thank you.
So Hannah, is this recording now?
Good, okay.
First of all, Hannah sent out a notice that had a bibliography, and I'll add another one to it.
For those of you who are interested in our ancestors, there's a wonderful book called Zen's Chinese Heritage by Andy Ferguson.
We'll send out the note for it.
That and the Roaring Stream give you a lot of primary materials to go to if you're interested in following any of these tracks that appear.
I offer [unclear: "each side"] to begin with a story about sure do, who was saying, I keep coming back to it: what meets the eye is the way.
This next story really begins with his teacher, Ching Yuan, who was the immediate Dharma heir of Queen Ng, our sixth patriarch and really the foundation of our Zen tradition.
It turns out that Ching Yuan was the author of the famous description of Zen, fully reminiscent of the old Donovan song.
He said:
*Before I began the study of Zen, mountains were mountains and waters were waters.
When I first achieved some insight into the truth of Zen, through the benevolence of my teacher, Queen Ng, mountains were no longer mountains and waters no longer waters.
But now that I've attained full enlightenment, I'm at rest and mountains are once again mountains and waters are waters.*

So sure do was one of Ching Yuan's students, and he not only practiced meditation but also studied the Chinese translations of Buddhist texts from India, as well as Indian and Chinese commentaries on those scriptures.
Here's a little story about sure do's awakening.
It came about as a result of his reading a passage that said:
*Only those can be called holy, who view the world in such a way that they see themselves in all things.*
Sure do had a sudden insight that this statement did not go far enough.
He slammed his fist on the table, exclaiming:
*A sage has no self, yet there is nothing that is not the self.
The body of reality is formless, who speaks of self and others.*
*The round mirror is marvelously bright.
All things and the mysteries of their being appear in it simultaneously.
Objects and knowledge are not one, who says they come or go to one another.
How true are the words of this treatise.*
You read that and you can't help but think about what we chant from Dogen, 500 years later, where he says:
*To study the way is to be actualized by myriad things.
When actualized by myriad things, your body and mind as well as the bodies and minds of others drop away.
No trace of enlightenment remains.
And this no trace continues endlessly.*
It turns out that just after sure do had this realization, he fell asleep, and he had a dream.
In this dream he was with his teacher, who he was with when he was 13, the sixth ancestor Huineng.
They were riding on the back of a great tortoise that was swimming in the big ocean.
He woke up and surmised that the tortoise symbolized wisdom and that the sea was the sea of existence.
He took the dream to mean that he, together with the sixth ancestor, sat upon wisdom's back swimming in the sea of existence.
That realization inspired him to write the chant that we have in our service, the merging of difference and unity.
So from his dream of riding on the tortoise's back we have the merging of difference and unity that we chant most Saturday mornings as part of our service.
That's just a little background for sure do and how he came to this grass hut that we're studying.
Let us now consider his room that includes the entire world.
Tonight the assignment was to read the last stanza.
We're going to skip the last line because it ties better into the succeeding stanza, so we're going to deal with the first four lines tonight.

*Though the hut is small, it includes the entire world.* *In 10 square feet an old man illumines forms and their nature.* *A great vehicle Bodhisattva trusts without doubt.* *The middling or lowly can't help wondering.*
Let me offer you a couple of alternative translations.
This is a tricky passage, and there are lots of ways it can be read.
One translation says:
*This little shack contains the entire universe and my physical body is integrated with it.*
That's different from what we have in our translation.
Another translation says:
*Although the thatch hut is small, it contains the Dharma realm.
The Dharma [unclear: "due to in"] a square 10 feet and old man studies liberation of the essential body.*
In the Dogen study group with Chris Burkhart, we read a couple of different translations of Dogen.
It's astonishing how the message is the same, but it's like it's all ice cream and they're really different flavors.
This struck me as a similar situation.

When I sat with my friend Paul Hansen, the Chinese scholar, he said you can read the line about the empty room as: the old man internalizes his understanding of aspects, or he embodies in his heart an understanding of mutuality, or he understands with his inmost being.
This forms in their nature is really one way of looking at these characters, because obviously these four translators have looked at them each quite differently.
Down to the details: the hut is small, that's pretty straightforward, but including the entire world.
In the Chinese, the first character means law or rules and the second character means the world or the domain.
Phonetically the second character means big, and the radical or the root of that character is a square divided in four parts, which means field, or the Buddha field as we would know it.
That's the field beyond form and emptiness that we chant in our robe chant.
So this "includes the entire world" means it also contains everything, but in the context of this poem it also contains nothing: forms and emptiness coming together here simultaneously.
Here it gets really interesting, when it talks about "in ten square feet an old man illumines forms and their nature."
Literally, it does say 10 square feet.
One of the things I did before I sat with my friend Paul was pull up each character from Chinese, put it on the screen and do a Google search, and it'll give you a dictionary meaning for it.
So it says, yeah, 101010 feet.
But it turns out the first time Paul read that, and he hadn't seen this poem before, he read those characters as [unclear: "fun john"].
He said that means Abbott.
This is really fascinating, but we can say okay, we've got a little room inhabited by a senior Dharma practitioner.
Simultaneously we've gone from "I've built a grass hut" to the person who inhabits this hut, and now suddenly we're an old man sitting calmly in the second verse, a contemplative old man.
How did we age so quickly?
What happened?
Within three [unclear: "stances"] we've gone from a vigorous person building a grass hut on a big flat rock to an old man sitting contemplating forms in their nature.
In one sense it captures the whole cycle of our lives, from self-sufficient builder to a Whitman-like character lying around and having his meal and burping and taking a nap.
And "their natures": what natures are they, and how specific?
But this is where it gets really interesting.
I'm going to read you a little document that I found.
It refers to Vimalakirti's room.

The Vimalakirti Sutra is one of the primary texts of our tradition, and Vimalakirti and Layman [unclear: "pong"] are the two lay people in our tradition who are enlightened, and the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas look to them for examples of how to live this life.
In the Vimalakirti Sutra the Buddha keeps asking the different Bodhisattvas to go visit Vimalakirti, and they keep saying, "I can't do it.
I heard him at the market talking, and he's a lot smarter than I am.
He knows the Dharma better than I."
Finally the Buddha asks Manjushri, the Bodhisattva of wisdom, to go visit, and Manjushri says okay, he'll do it.
So here's just background for this 10 square foot room.

*When Manjushri agrees to visit Vimalakirti and engage in dialogue, all the disciples and Bodhisattvas, including those who had declined to visit him, suddenly decide they want to go and observe this spectacle: Dharma combat, Bodhisattva and human.

Manjushri arrives accompanied not only by the main disciples and Bodhisattvas, but by a great many heavenly and other extraordinary beings, all eager to witness the conversation of these two Bodhisattvas renowned for their wisdom.
Vimalakirti, with his special powers, is aware of their impending arrival and magically transforms a single room house into emptiness.
Although the room is small, all the myriad Bodhisattvas, disciples and spirits miraculously are able to find space in it.
This room is large; it contains the world.
Vimalakirti tells Manjushri that his room is empty because all Buddha fields are empty, and that all Buddha fields are empty even of emptiness, because all imaginings and views are empty.*
*And here Shri Putra shows up again, gets to play the dummy role.
He wonders where all the guests will sit, since there are no chairs in the room.
Knowing Shri Putra's thoughts, Vimalakirti asks him if he came for the Dharma or for a place to sit.
Shri Putra, always the target of Vimalakirti's sharp tongue, avows that he came for the Dharma, not for a chair.
And Vimalakirti chastises him, saying that one truly interested in the Dharma of Buddhas is not concerned about his own body, much less a chair.*
And here's where it really gets interesting.
In the seventh century, and I'm reading this as post-Zhuanzang, the fellow who went and got all his scriptures from India and brought them back to China:

*the Vimalakirti Sutra was so highly valued in China that a Chinese imperial envoy made a pilgrimage to the supposed site of Vimalakirti's house in northern India to measure the ruined foundations of the room, where this miraculous scene was supposed to have transpired.
The ruins that were shown to the envoy were one square zhang, or fang zhang, which is about 10 square feet.
Thereafter, Vimalakirti's room was referred to by this term throughout East Asia.
Vimalakirti's room size established the model for all Chan, Zen, Abbot's quarters, which are still named fang zhang in Chinese or hojo in Japanese after Vimalakirti's room.*
So I found that just one term, this 10 square foot room, opens up this whole universe of the Dharma, let alone what we would normally think of and say, oh, this room contains everything.
We can sort of extrapolate on that and understand from our understanding of teachings what that tells us.
But there's a deeper story here.
The second line that stands is:
*A great vehicle bodhisattva, trust without doubt; the middling or lowly can't help but wondering.*
So let's go back here.
Any comments or thoughts about this hut as small, including the entire world, the 10 square feet, and the old man [unclear: "aluminum"] forms and their nature, given the little background here?
The floor is open for thoughts or responses.
They ended up giving Abbots a little more space than 10 square feet.
They ended up getting 10 tatami mats.
Spacious.
And when you're interacting with [unclear: "Huitzu"] Suzuki, you probably called him Hojo-san, right?
It's the same, it's all the same term.
**Participant:** I was thinking about the hut as small.
It includes the entire world.
We are individually small, but we include the entire world.
Our mind is sort of like the mind-only teachings about what is the nature of reality.
And then in the second line, in the 10 square feet, an old man, an accomplished teacher, is enlightened by the forms and their nature.
He sees through to the perfection of all things.
So our minds light up the world.
In that interaction, the world lights up, everything lights up.
And keep that in mind when you read the passage about the shining window below the pine trees.
**Joden Bob Rose:** Okay.
Chris?
**Participant:** There is a story about several Confucian scholars visiting a Taoist sage who is sitting naked in his hut and meditating.
So they walk into his hut and they yell at him, "What are you doing sitting there without your pants on?"
And he says, "The whole world is my body.
This little hut is just my underwear.
What are you doing in my underpants?"
This is just what comes up with a little hut: that everything is included in everything else.
**Joden Bob Rose:** Yeah.
So another interesting piece of this is that the characters that we're reading as "contains the entire world" actually are translated there again.
Again, a combined character means the Dharma world.
So one of the translators picked that thought up: absolute reality, or the great field of the Buddha.
So again, there are layers and layers here of how we can read these characters and these lines.
Other thoughts?
**Participant:** Well, it's consistent, you know, the hut containing the entire world.
It's consistent with what Dogen says about no need to go off to the dusty realms.
You know, everything you need is right in your life now to practice and study.
I like Chapter 10, where they talked a lot about how it's where you are.
It doesn't matter if you're in the 10 foot hut or if you're on a park bench.
It's all about your mind.
I've been really aware of that, but I just like how he said that.
It is to take the knowledge of basically that everything's connected, and we're a small piece, like I think it was Edwina said, a small piece of the whole.
So I like the idea of a 10 foot hut anyway, but I liked it when he talked about how it doesn't have to be the 10 foot hut.
It can be the park bench, wherever you are.
So that's what I wanted to say.
**Participant:** I've been thinking that the hut is sort of how he's putting his practice into the world.
The hut is his conception of practice, the way he's practicing.
So his practice is this unsubstantial grass hut.
It's very delicate, but he's built it.
He's built his practice and maintains it.
And these descriptions of the hut are sort of like descriptions really of his practice.

Not so much an inside or an outside or a place, like things are happening over here or over there, or this person is here or there, but more like the hut is a grand metaphor for how he exists in the world as a practitioner.
Maybe this is the same thing, but I'm interpreting the hut as being me.
The small me, and then that it includes the entire world.
I include the entire world.
That's also what I've been feeling with this: the hut is more a metaphor for the [unclear: "sure"], himself, or for us as we're reading it.
And this is our constructive self.
It's my feeling as well that the hut is our mind and all the different aspects of our mind, from the weeds to the identity with self to the no identity and the entire world.
Last time we talked about the change from the first person to the third person.
And I was just noticing that it starts out, "I've built a grass hut where there's nothing of value."
So that's in the first person mode.
And then down here, it includes the entire world in ten feet square.
An old man [unclear: "alums forms in their nature"].
And so there's a transformation there, maybe.
And the previous stance, the person in the house, has gone from "I built" to the person to an old man.
This was saying the introduction is this whole lifecycle that's going on here, or at least in the imagination of what a person is.
So, yeah.
I thought about the ten by ten, and how it's much easier to control something that's ten by ten, and to really think about what's in your ten by ten.
And I like that Ben Connolly talked about the Internet and news and all the things that we let in.
And then I was thinking about controlling that, and you can only control what's in yourself.
But then I was thinking about what you said on the weekend about you affecting change globally for the environment.
And how maybe we all put on our masks in the airplane first.
So get that ten by ten working well, and then affect change on the bigger ten by ten.
I thought about the line that says a great vehicle Bodhisattva trusts without doubt.
And what we know is that that is the Mahayana path.
And that's what we are following.
And then that he trusts without doubt.
And that means that he's not abiding in hindrance.
He's somehow managed to free himself and trust, not be bogged down by wondering if it's all right or not.
So before we jump into those lines, is there some stuff there as well?
Any further thoughts, at least in this moment, on those first opening lines of this stanza?
I wanted to add, you introduced the Donovan song.
First there's a moment.
But if you look at the very first verse, he's an I.
I am doing this.
I am doing that.
So he's got this self.
In the second verse he's no longer a person.
He's just a person.
There is no mountain in that second verse.
And he says places worldly people live, he doesn't live.
So he's on the top of the pole, the ten foot pole.
And then in the third verse, he's back.
He's back into the world.
He's an old man.
But yet he's now illumined, forms.
And he's in that third verse as an old man, an old wise man.
So parallel to that, [unclear: "sure do"] has gone beyond his teachers' Dharma and is proposing a further Dharma.
That would be one way to look at this in terms of the succession of ancestors.
Each teacher absorbs the previous teacher and goes beyond.

One of the commentaries, Joan Southerland, one of the articles, "Koans for Troubled Times," makes the point that one of the breakthroughs of [unclear: "sure do"] and Matsu, his Dharma brother, is that it's really the first time that people start talking and recognizing Zen as a person to person intimate connection and not as an abstract discussion.
So I think, Kate, what you're bringing up is really appropriate, because this is really making it human in a way that earlier teachers weren't quite as intimate with anyone else.
Go ahead.
Yeah, I'm finding that the metaphor of the grass hut is very, very interesting, and I'm not sure what it means or says.
So I see it as, let's say, life.
And then what we do with life, we [unclear: "drink interpretation"] to it.
And we look at its size.
And we notice that it's a certain size.
And it's this.
And it's not that.
And there was something interesting going on there.
So the grass hut is a grass hut.
And then we start measuring it and interpreting it.
And something that he apparently said to one of his students, in question of whether a difference and sameness.
And the teacher's comment was, well, if you said it's the same, I teach you the difference.
And if you said it was different, I teach you the same.
So there's something about what is, and then there's how we interpret it, how we see it, and what we add to it.
So a great vehicle Bodhisattva, as Hannah was laying out the line, trusts without doubt.
And then there's this problematic line that Ben is troubled by in his interpretation, the middling or lowly can't help but wondering.

So one alternative translation, which has, I think, an unfortunate first line, goes: *Great Bodhisattvas don't doubt my ideas.* Which I think is a little bit inverted, but then the second line is: *though humans may think them strange.* So it's not putting it into a hierarchy but simply they're odd.
So, a couple of interesting things to me, again putting this through the Chinese translation.
These characters come out as [unclear: "a poo and saw"], which if you just read the dictionary [unclear: "music"] something like a fragrant, a fragrant Buddhist god or an immortal.
But Pusa is how the Chinese translated the Sanskrit for Bodhisattva.
So, in the Chinese, Pusa, Bodhisattva.
And again, as we've pointed out earlier, we now have this transformation from the I to he, the person, to this old man, but they're all now identified in that sense as practicing Mahayana Buddhism.
This Bodhisattva trusts without doubt.

And so, as Hannah was beginning to point out, Mahayana Buddhism is committed to not entering Nirvana even if they could, but to return to the body in this life to save all beings and all delusions, enter all Dharma gates and become the Buddha way.
Given that vow being taken to follow the Bodhisattva way.
How can we even begin to hold abiding doubts?
And as Ben points out, trust here is about a condition of consciousness that's completely at ease, an absence of anxiety about being at rest.

So again, the word that's translated as trust here in our translation can also be translated as: you have full confidence in something, you have proof of something, it's guaranteed, or that you're also a messenger or an envoy for something.
So again, these characters have these multiple meanings that can point in the same direction but have different edges to them.

And again, as at the beginning when [unclear: "sure"] just says, "I built a grass hut where there's nothing of value," the character for nothing is [unclear: "move or woo"] in Chinese, [unclear: "move emptiness"].
Well, here again, the great vehicle Bodhisattva trust [unclear: "move"] empty of doubt.
It's translated in our translations as "without doubt," but the character is "empty."
So again, there are these deep resonances with our Mahayana teachings.
**Joden Bob Rose:** And as was brought up earlier, how empty is this Bodhisattva?
How empty are we ourselves?
What measure do we use to define what our heart space is, as Todd was measuring?
What's our capacity for emptiness and for containing everything?
And then, as someone else mentioned, this character for doubt can also be translated as obstruction or a hindrance.
So, *shudo* is the merging of difference and unity.
There are four lines in there that I think tie directly to this.
When he asked, *if you don't understand the way right before you, you know the path as you walk.

Progress is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.* So in a sense he's really saying that because we are practicing in this tradition, and we are taking the vow to be a Bodhisattva, we recognize hindrances as a construction of our own minds.
If we are practicing fully, there are no hindrances to our actions and to our understanding.
It also brought up for me, as we chant in the Heart Sutra, *with nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajnaparamita, and thus the mind is without hindrance.
Without hindrance there's no fear.

Far beyond all inverted views, one realizes Nirvana.* And Red Pine's translation of the Heart Sutra, that last line, says *they're well without walls in the mind, and thus without fears, and finally see through Nirvana.* So there's a whole complex of issues that come up with saying that the Bodhisattva trusts without doubt.
Then the second line of this couplet: middling or lowly can't help but wonder.

All I'd offer in relation to Ben Connolly's thoughts is that my friend Paul, translating this, said that people of middling roots or capacity will hear it and give rise to strange, incorrect feelings.
The point he made is that at this point in Chinese history, and in the evolution of Buddhism in China, Mahayana was still a pretty strange doctrine.
It was pushing an envelope that made a lot of people uncomfortable.

So if we don't take it as a hierarchical critique, as Ben makes it out, the higher and the lower, but simply as a doctrine that in some ways is hard to understand and harder to comprehend, it's a kinder spin on it than may appear on its face.
What's interesting, again, is that when we're talking about inner, outer or in between, that in-between character is a square with a line through it, and that's the same middle that's spoken to here.
It's the same character.
I'm not sure how to think about that except as the middle way.
The Taoists were sometimes having trouble with the Mahayana Buddhist concept as well.
Some of them embraced it and some were more interested in achieving eternal life.
I'm not a scholar of this, but there are probably many different ways to look at these characters and spin them differently than simply as a hierarchical sense of intelligence.
So let's open this one up to the floor, because there are lots of places to dig here.
**Participant:** Well, I just wanted to say that I actually found this to be one of the more disappointing chapters in the commentary, because some of this you have to look at in historical context.
Both India and Japan had full-on caste systems during this time period.
Although in China you could move up by taking your exams and become a higher-up in the hierarchy, the cultures that this is generated from had very strict hierarchies.
We are Western liberals and we don't like hierarchy, so we reject this, but this came directly out of a society that was very hierarchical.
So I don't think it's a bad thing that it's in the poem.
I think that's the world he lived in.
Yes, I'm thinking about the Bodhisattva trusts without doubt, but the people who are uncomfortable with the Bodhisattva really wonder: is he going to perish or not?
Does he really come back?
Does he really stay forever and ever to save all beings?
That's a big natural question for anybody learning Buddhism, I think.
It strikes me that they're not so much not advanced in their understanding, but that's a question that people go through.

How do you reconcile all sentient beings, et cetera, these impossible vows, and the unimaginable thing of returning always and never getting to nirvana and never dying because everyone has to be saved?
So I think it's speaking more to that.
We can apply this to our own lives.
We can see this line as us: the higher way, the middle way and the low way are just different facets of us.
When we're not at our best, when we're not being most skillful, then that is when we are under the poison of doubt.
Good.
That's where I was coming to with this chapter, with this line: that part of ourselves that can't help but judge or worry or be anxious about outcome.
I sort of read these lines as being paired: the practitioner, and someone who is set up as being not the practitioner.
The practitioner is someone who trusts and has no sense of obstruction in their practice within the hut.
But the person who's outside of that has doubt, wondering: is this practice really substantial?
Does it really mean anything?
Is it coming and going?
Is it easy?
Does it really have any kind of hope for the world, or is it a flash in the pan?
All the creeping doubts that keep us at arm's length from our practice and not fully present.
I think if we can practice without doubt, it helps us to move past our fear and anxiety.
That is our human nature.
Like he talked about, the fear can be helpful to protect us.
We can use that to protect ourselves.
But then we get fearful about things that haven't happened yet, or things we don't have control over, the stories that our minds tell us.
So if we can let go of that and not have the doubt, then we don't have to suffer with the fear and anxiety when it doesn't serve us.
What resonated with me was just: don't have doubt that reality will happen.
It's okay with whatever it is, and not to judge that one way or the other.
Then you'll be more at ease if you can let go of that fear and anxiety and trust reality.
So trusting reality is a good segue to breakout rooms.
I think Hannah's got the technology this time, so I've got a couple of questions for you to consider.
They reflect some of the questions, or thoughts, that came up in the last few minutes.
How have you made your little everywhere your little hut, a practice space?
How secure is it, and is it perishable or not?
How do you embody your practice?
Where does it go when you're not at home, when you're traveling in far countries, or when you're going to the store?
And what doubts arise about your life, about your practice, and about Zen?
Three questions come out of this for me that you can think about in any way that feels appropriate.
How do you make your practice space?
How do you embody your practice, how do you carry it with you?
The poet I mentioned in my talk the other day, Charles Olson, has a great line.
He says, "He who carries his house on his head is in heaven."
So how do you carry your heart with you?
How do you visit your heart, and what's the relationship between that?
And how do doubts arise about your life, your practice, about Zen, and how do you grapple with those doubts?
So, Hannah will break us up and break us out, and we'll be back in 10 minutes and have a few minutes for people to reflect and to present a thought that comes out of these questions.
Then we'll bow out and take a break and then have our evening service.

Right.
Yeah, you're saying you're concerned, that came back to those lines from the Heart Sutra, which we had talked about.

Yeah.
All these years of striving.
That's what I love about your choice of the material: it's a completely different look at just being.
Right, they always say, just sit, but there's permission to lighten up, I guess.
